{{Short description|Concept in quantum information theory}}
In [[quantum information theory]], '''quantum state purification''' refers to the process of representing a [[Mixed state (physics)|mixed state]] as a [[Pure state|pure quantum state]] of higher-dimensional [[Hilbert space]]. The purification allows the original mixed state to be recovered by taking the [[partial trace]] over the additional degrees of freedom. The purification is not unique, the different purifications that can lead to the same mixed states are limited by the '''Schrödinger–HJW theorem'''. 

Purification is used in algorithms such as [[entanglement distillation]], [[magic state distillation]] and [[algorithmic cooling]].

== Description ==
Let <math>\mathcal H_S</math> be a [[finite-dimensional]] [[complex number|complex]] [[Hilbert space]], and consider a generic (possibly [[Quantum state#Mixed states|mixed]]) [[quantum state]] <math>\rho</math> defined on <math>\mathcal H_S</math> and admitting a decomposition of the form
<math display="block">\rho = \sum_i p_i|\phi_i\rangle\langle\phi_i|</math>
for a collection of (not necessarily mutually orthogonal) states <math>|\phi_i\rangle \in \mathcal H_S</math> and coefficients <math>p_i \ge 0</math> such that <math display="inline">\sum_i p_i = 1</math>. Note that any quantum state can be written in such a way for some <math>\{|\phi_i\rangle\}_i</math> and <math>\{p_i\}_i</math>.<ref>{{Citation |last=Nielsen |first=Michael A. |title=The Schmidt decomposition and purifications |url=https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511976667.006 |work=Quantum Computation and Quantum Information |pages=110–111 |place=Cambridge |publisher=Cambridge University Press |access-date= |last2=Chuang |first2=Isaac L.}}.</ref> 

Any such <math>\rho</math> can be ''purified'', that is, represented as the [[partial trace]] of a [[pure state]] defined in a larger Hilbert space. More precisely, it is always possible to find a (finite-dimensional) Hilbert space <math>\mathcal H_A</math> and a pure state <math>|\Psi_{SA}\rangle \in \mathcal H_S \otimes \mathcal H_A</math> such that <math>\rho = \operatorname{Tr}_A\big(|\Psi_{SA}\rangle\langle\Psi_{SA}|\big)</math>. Furthermore, the states <math>|\Psi_{SA}\rangle</math> satisfying this are all and only those of the form
<math display="block">|\Psi_{SA}\rangle = \sum_i \sqrt{p_i} |\phi_i\rangle \otimes |a_i\rangle</math>
for some orthonormal basis <math>\{|a_i\rangle\}_i \subset \mathcal H_A</math>. The state <math>|\Psi_{SA}\rangle</math> is then referred to as the "purification of <math>\rho</math>". Since the auxiliary space and the basis can be chosen arbitrarily, the purification of a mixed state is not unique; in fact, there are infinitely many purifications of a given mixed state.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Watrous |first=John |author-link1=John Watrous (computer scientist) |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/theory-of-quantum-information/AE4AA5638F808D2CFEB070C55431D897 |title=The Theory of Quantum Information |date=2018|publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-107-18056-7 |location=Cambridge |doi=10.1017/9781316848142}}</ref> Because all of them admit a decomposition in the form given above, given any pair of purifications <math>|\Psi\rangle, |\Psi'\rangle \in \mathcal H_S \otimes \mathcal H_A</math>, there is always some unitary operation <math>U : \mathcal H_A \to \mathcal H_A</math> such that
<math display="block">|\Psi'\rangle = (I\otimes U) |\Psi\rangle.</math>

== Schrödinger–HJW theorem ==
The '''Schrödinger–HJW theorem''' is a result about the realization of a [[Mixed state (physics)|mixed state]] of a [[quantum system]] as an [[statistical ensemble|ensemble]] of [[pure quantum state]]s and the relation between the corresponding purifications of the [[density matrix|density operators]]. The theorem is named after [[Erwin Schrödinger]] who proved it in 1936,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Schrödinger |first=Erwin |year=1936 |title=Probability relations between separated systems |journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]] |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=446–452 |bibcode=1936PCPS...32..446S |doi=10.1017/S0305004100019137 |authorlink1=Erwin Schrödinger}}</ref> and after [[Lane P. Hughston]], [[Richard Jozsa]] and [[William Wootters]] who rediscovered in 1993.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hughston |first=Lane P. |last2=Jozsa |first2=Richard |last3=Wootters |first3=William K. |date=November 1993 |title=A complete classification of quantum ensembles having a given density matrix |journal=[[Physics Letters A]] |volume=183 |issue=1 |pages=14–18 |bibcode=1993PhLA..183...14H |doi=10.1016/0375-9601(93)90880-9 |issn=0375-9601}}</ref> The result was also found independently (albeit partially) by Nicolas Hadjisavvas building upon work by [[Edwin Thompson Jaynes|E. T. Jaynes]] of 1957,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hadjisavvas |first=Nicolas |year=1981 |title=Properties of mixtures on non-orthogonal states |journal=[[Letters in Mathematical Physics]] |volume=5 |issue=4 |pages=327–332 |bibcode=1981LMaPh...5..327H |doi=10.1007/BF00401481}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Jaynes |first=E. T. |year=1957 |title=Information theory and statistical mechanics. II |journal=[[Physical Review]] |volume=108 |pages=171–190 |bibcode=1957PhRv..108..171J |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.108.171 |number=2}}</ref> and [[Nicolas Gisin]] in 1989,<ref>Gisin, N. (1989). “Stochastic quantum dynamics and relativity”, Helvetica Physica Acta 62, 363–371.</ref> while a significant part of it was likewise independently discovered by [[N. David Mermin]] in 1999 who discovered the link with Schrödinger's work.<ref>{{cite book |last=Fuchs |first=Christopher A. |title=Coming of Age with Quantum Information: Notes on a Paulian Idea |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |year=2011 |isbn=978-0-521-19926-1 |location=Cambridge |oclc=535491156}}</ref> Thanks to its complicated history, it is also known by various other names such as the '''GHJW theorem''',<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mermin |first=N. David |author-link=N. David Mermin |date=1999 |title=What Do These Correlations Know about Reality? Nonlocality and the Absurd |journal=[[Foundations of Physics]] |volume=29 |issue=4 |pages=571–587 |arxiv=quant-ph/9807055 |bibcode=1998quant.ph..7055M |doi=10.1023/A:1018864225930}}</ref> the '''HJW theorem''', and the '''purification theorem'''.

Consider a mixed quantum state <math>\rho</math> with two different realizations as ensemble of pure states as <math display="inline">\rho = \sum_i p_i |\phi_i\rangle\langle\phi_i|</math> and <math display="inline">\rho = \sum_j q_j |\varphi_j\rangle\langle\varphi_j|</math>. Here both <math>|\phi_i\rangle</math>and <math>|\varphi_j\rangle</math> are not assumed to be mutually orthogonal. There will be two corresponding purifications of the mixed state <math>\rho</math> reading as follows:
: Purification 1: <math>|\Psi_{SA}^1\rangle=\sum_i\sqrt{p_i}|\phi_i\rangle \otimes |a_i\rangle</math>;
: Purification 2: <math>|\Psi_{SA}^2\rangle=\sum_j\sqrt{q_j}|\varphi_j\rangle \otimes |b_j\rangle</math>.

The sets <math>\{|a_i\rangle\}</math>and <math>\{|b_j\rangle\}</math> are two collections of orthonormal bases of the respective auxiliary spaces. These two purifications only differ by a unitary transformation acting on the auxiliary space, namely, there exists a unitary matrix <math>U_A</math> such that <math>|\Psi^1_{SA}\rangle = (I\otimes U_A)|\Psi^2_{SA}\rangle</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kirkpatrick |first=K. A. |date=February 2006 |title=The Schrödinger-HJW Theorem |journal=[[Foundations of Physics Letters]] |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=95–102 |doi=10.1007/s10702-006-1852-1 |issn=0894-9875 |arxiv=quant-ph/0305068 |bibcode=2006FoPhL..19...95K }}</ref> Therefore, <math display="inline">|\Psi_{SA}^1\rangle = \sum_j \sqrt{q_j}|\varphi_j\rangle\otimes U_A|b_j\rangle</math>, which means that we can realize the different ensembles of a mixed state just by making different measurements on the purifying system.
